title: CQRS event sourcing and tradeoffs
concepts: CQRS separates the model used to change data from the model used to query it; that separation can exist within one process and one database or across separately scaled stores.
A command expresses an intent to change state and can be accepted or rejected; a query returns data without changing state. CQRS organizes these responsibilities but does not require event sourcing.
Event sourcing stores an append-only sequence of domain changes as the system of record and derives current state by replaying those events; it is a persistence model, not merely publishing events.
Read projections are built from committed changes and may lag behind writes, so the design must make consistency delay visible and decide which operations need read-your-own-write behavior.
Event streams require explicit rules for ordering, optimistic concurrency, idempotent projection updates, schema evolution, replay, snapshots, and sensitive-data handling.
CQRS and event sourcing add operational and cognitive costs. Use them only when read/write divergence, audit history, temporal reconstruction, or independent scaling justifies those costs.
